subsystems.name: Servicer spacecraft bus
subsystems.role: carries the capture hardware to the target and survives years in low Earth orbit.

subsystems.name: Rendezvous and proximity navigation
subsystems.role: closes the gap from tens of kilometres to metres without ground intervention at the end.
parts: ground radar tracking and orbit determination

subsystems.name: Capture mechanism
subsystems.role: grapples an object that was never designed to be caught.
parts: magnetic or mechanical docking plate (only if the target carries one)

subsystems.name: Target characterisation
subsystems.role: works out the object's shape, mass distribution and tumble before touching it.

subsystems.name: Deorbit or disposal module
subsystems.role: provides the velocity change that drops the object's perigee into the atmosphere.
parts: high-thrust chemical engine and propellant tanks
drag sail or electrodynamic tether alternatives

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: tracks everything in orbit, plans the approach and manages licensing and liability.

buildSteps.title: Pick and track a target
buildSteps.detail: Choose a large, high-risk object — typically a defunct satellite or a spent upper stage of several tonnes — and track it for months to build an accurate orbit and brightness curve.

buildSteps.title: Design the servicer around it
buildSteps.detail: Mass, inertia, spin state and any usable attachment feature determine capture method, propellant load and structural strength.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate the spacecraft
buildSteps.detail: Build the bus, install avionics, propulsion and sensors, and integrate the capture mechanism.

buildSteps.title: Test on the ground
buildSteps.detail: Air-bearing tables and flat floors rehearse proximity manoeuvres; nets and harpoons are fired at representative targets; the whole spacecraft goes through thermal-vacuum and vibration testing.

buildSteps.title: Launch and commission
buildSteps.detail: Ride-share to a nearby orbit, then deploy solar arrays and check sensors, typically over several weeks.

buildSteps.title: Far-range rendezvous
buildSteps.detail: Ground navigation brings the servicer within a few tens of kilometres; onboard cameras take over and the distance is closed cautiously, with planned retreats if anything is uncertain.

buildSteps.title: Inspection and tumble matching
buildSteps.detail: The servicer holds station a few tens of metres away, builds a 3D model, then slowly matches the target's rotation so the two are effectively still relative to each other.

buildSteps.title: Capture
buildSteps.detail: A robotic arm grasps a structural feature, or a net or harpoon secures the body; the combined stack is then stabilised and its spin damped.

buildSteps.title: Disposal
buildSteps.detail: The servicer burns to lower the target's perigee to roughly 200–300 km so it re-enters within about 25 years, then either rides down with it or releases it and moves to the next target — and itself disposes safely at end of life.

prerequisites.why: you cannot remove what you cannot find and re-find; radar and optical networks already track objects down to about 10 cm in low Earth orbit.
the final metres must be flown faster than ground commands can loop, and no servicer has yet docked with a large unprepared object unattended.
nets and harpoons have flown in demonstrations, but none has yet secured a multi-tonne derelict and deorbited it.
removing a heavy object from low Earth orbit costs hundreds of metres per second of velocity change; that drives the size and price of the servicer.
a large object released to re-enter may not burn up completely, so casualty risk has to be calculated and mitigated.

pathway.milestone: commercial servicers flying close-approach demonstrations against real derelicts
pathway.unlocks: proof that rendezvous and inspection of an uncooperative object works.

pathway.milestone: first funded removal of a single large object — capturing it and lowering its orbit
pathway.unlocks: a demonstrated unit cost per object removed.

pathway.milestone: multi-target 'sweeper' missions carrying several deorbit kits to successive objects, or magnetic docking plates fitted to new satellites before launch
pathway.unlocks: removal at a cost per kilogram that operators could plausibly pay.

pathway.milestone: routine removal funded by a fee on every satellite launched, targeting the largest derelicts first
pathway.unlocks: stabilising the low-orbit population before collisions outpace the natural decay of debris.
